title: How do you answer "How would you find that out?" in a case interview?
description: "How would you find that out?" for case interviews. When the interviewer asks how you would get data. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: Answer "How would you find that out?" by naming two or three sources that fit the question: ask customers, ask experts, use existing data, or run a small test. Then say what result would confirm or reject your idea, because that is what turns research into a decision.
body:
When it helps

Interviewers ask this when the data is not in the case, or to see whether you can be practical: "How would you know customers would pay more?" or "How would you find out why sales fell?" It also strengthens hypothesis-driven answers, because every hypothesis needs a way to test it.

The checklist

Ask customers

  • Surveys
  • Interviews and focus groups
  • Pilots and A/B tests

Ask experts

  • The client's own specialists (sales, operations, finance)
  • Industry experts, suppliers, distributors

Use data

  • The client's own data: sales, transactions, costs
  • Industry reports and official statistics
  • Competitors' prices and public results

An example: will customers pay for faster delivery?

You could survey customers, talk to the delivery team about what customers ask for, and check what rivals charge for express delivery. The strongest answer adds a cheap, fast test, because people often say one thing in a survey and do another at the checkout.

Say an online shop offers express delivery to two similar groups of 1,000 customers, at different prices (illustrative results):

PriceTake-upExpress ordersRevenue
$4.9920%200$998
$7.9912%120$959

The higher price brings in slightly less revenue and serves fewer customers, so $4.99 wins unless each express delivery costs much more to run. No survey would have told you that as reliably.

Match the method to the question

A supermarket's premium ready meals have stopped selling. First, define what needs explaining: fewer shoppers visiting the aisle, fewer buying once they see the products, buying less often, or switching to a rival. Then pick evidence for each:

  • Transaction data shows when and where sales fell, and whether prices or promotions changed.
  • Store visits reveal empty shelves or poor placement.
  • Short customer interviews reveal views on quality and price.
  • Competitor checks spot new launches or discounts at the same time.

Then a sharp test: compare similar stores that kept the meals in stock with those that ran out. If the fall is concentrated in stores with gaps on the shelf, availability becomes the leading explanation.

How it sounds in an interview

"I'd find out in three ways: check our sales data to see where and when it changed, talk to a few store managers, and run a small test. If the drop is concentrated in stores with stock problems, that points to supply rather than demand."

The weak version is "I'd do some market research": no source, no method and no idea what result would matter.

Common mistakes

  • Defaulting to surveys, which tell you what people say, not what they do.
  • Listing sources without saying what each would show.
  • Asking for more data without saying how it would change the decision.

Practise it

1. How would you find out whether a gym's members are leaving because of a new competitor?

Show the answer

Check cancellations by month against the competitor's opening date, and by distance from the new gym. Ask leavers why in a short exit survey. If cancellations rose only among members living near the rival after it opened, the competitor is the likely cause.

2. How would you estimate how many people would use a new bus route?

Show the answer

Use travel data on journeys between the areas the route links, ridership on similar existing routes, and a short survey of residents. Then run a trial with a limited timetable and set a ridership target for keeping it.
